items.title: The week everything fell apart
items.summary:
There was a dayslong Outlook outage. A nationwide ground stop for only the second time in 25 years. Banks seemed to suddenly stop working. Even iCloud couldn't stay up and running. This week, it felt like the technological world simply collapsed. And it felt like this might be the beginning of something even bigger.
On this episode of The Vergecast, Nilay and David go through the week's many calamities, and try to explain both what happened in each case - which was generally much milder than the conspiracy theories would have you believe - and why all these small issues might still add up to something worth worrying about. Signal is blocking Gemini and Siri AI from reading your screen
items.summary:
Signal users on iOS will see this option to toggle blocking screenshots and preventing Siri AI from scanning on-screen content. | Image: Signal	

Signal is restricting the ability to take screenshots on Android and iOS devices in an effort to prevent AI agents from reading users' messages and other data. The agentic AI capabilities built into operating systems that analyze on-screen information to learn more about the user are "undermining Signal's ability to independently guarantee privacy," Signal president Meredith Whittaker said in a blog post, while urging OS providers to make it easier for app developers to control what data agents can access.

items.title: Why the robots are ditching Uber
items.summary:
In a late August earnings call, Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi sounded optimistic about his company's "very strong" partnership with Waymo, the global leader in autonomous robotaxis. The two companies had been working together for years in several cities - including exclusively in Austin and Atlanta - and things were going swimmingly, according to Khosrowshahi.
"We believe we'll continue to operate next year in those marketplaces," he gushed. "It's a terrific product, and the on-the-ground partnership continues to be very strong."

Apple is hiring engineers to build its own AI agent
items.summary:
Apple is working on its own AI agent that can perform a range of tasks for you, including browsing the web, working across apps, writing code, and calling services. That's according to a job listing spotted by Bloomberg, which says Apple is looking for an engineer to lead the creation of an agentic AI assistant.
An AI agent from Apple would put the iPhone maker in the running to compete with the likes of Meta's Muse, OpenAI's Dots, Anthropic's Duet, and Google's Tasks. Muse, ChatGPT, and Perplexity can already take control of a computer through their Mac apps, while Google just started letting Gemini do the same.

items.title: A brief history of Nvidia’s recent stock fluctuations
items.summary:
Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange during morning trading on November 18, 2026 in New York City. | Image: Getty Images	

"We've got this," Colette Kress, interim CEO of Nvidia, said Tuesday night as she closed out the embattled chip company's third quarter earnings call.
By Thursday, the company's stock price was hovering at around $150 per share, a nearly 40 percent drop from its all-time high on October 6th, and wiping out a brief post-earnings pop on Tuesday night. Meanwhile, Wall Street was paying up for one of Nvidia's biggest customers as Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut at $111.50 per share - 34 percent higher than expected.

items.title: Meta’s Muse Charm might cost $300
items.summary:
Meta is planning to price the Muse Charm, a little gadget with a screen that lets you chat with your Muse AI agent, at $300, according to The Information. CEO Mark Zuckerberg revealed the gadget earlier this year and said the company expected to ship the Charm "in time for the holidays in December," but he didn't provide a price at the time.
When he announced the Muse Charm, Zuckerberg said that the company had "packed the whole Muse experience," including real-time voice and avatar technology, into the gadget. It has a fingerprint sensor, and you can tap it to be able to talk to a Muse AI agent without unlocking a phone or opening an app.  …

items.title: Google is putting AI chats right on the homepage
items.summary:
Google is updating its homepage to include AI searches. In a post on X, Google's vice president of product, Robby Stein, shows how you can now open a collapsible sidebar to view and continue your AI chats.
Based on the GIF shared by Stein, it looks like you can open the sidebar by clicking the gray bar that appears on the left side of your screen. From there, Google will show a list of the searches you've made using AI Mode, along with the ability to start a new thread, search your threads, or connect a Gemini Notebook.

items.title: FCC greenlights rule allowing prisons to jam cellphone signals
items.summary:
The Federal Communications Commission voted unanimously to allow state and local prisons to jam cellphones. In an announcement on Thursday, the FCC argues the rule will help combat an "influx of contraband cellphones" used to carry out crimes from prison.
Jammers are generally banned under Section 333 of the Communications Act of 1934, though they're used at some federal facilities. FCC Chair Brendan Carr claims that giving correctional facilities access to this technology will help prevent prisoners from using phones for illegal activity. items.title: Sony’s WH-1000XM5 are cheaper than ever for Black Friday
items.summary:
All four colors of the WH-1000XM5 are in stock at the discounted price.	

Back in my day, the only “Doorbuster” sales were at physical retail stores. But now, you can get ultra-low prices before Black Friday whether you want to shop in-store or online. One that stands out is the previous-generation Sony WH-1000XM5 noise-canceling headphones, which are marked down to their lowest price ever, just $169.99 at Best Buy. While their MSRP is $399.99, they’ve been spotted as low as $198 in the last few months.
Sony WH-1000XM5

Where to Buy:

 $399.99 $198 at Amazon
 $399.99 $198 at Best Buy
 $399.99 $199.99 at Costco

The WH-1000XM5 launched in 2022, and despite having been succeeded by the WH-1000XM6, they’re still an excellent set of headphones. Their active noise cancellation effect is one of the best out there — competitive with the latest models from Bose and Apple — and the sound profile is tighter and more balanced than the older Sony headphones. There are some minor downsides, like a bulky case and all-plastic design, but those seem easier to overlook at this lower price point.
The newer Sony WH-1000XM6 improve the sound and noise cancellation, with quality of life upgrades not present in the XM5, like a folding design and more comfortable headband. However, they’re significantly more expensive, currently discounted to $348 during Black Friday (Amazon, Best Buy), down from their MSRP of $450. 
To make shopping a little more confusing, the newer WH-1000XM4C sit between the XM5 and XM6 in terms of price, and are a slightly updated version of the older XM4 model with its foldable design. Our reviewer John Higgins thinks the XM4C’s noise cancellation lags behind, so I’d opt for the XM5 over them, especially at the sale price.
